evals.prompt: I run developer experience at Ledgerline, a B2B payouts API. Engineering keeps an OpenAPI 3.1 spec current from code annotations - 52 operations in it today. Our public reference at docs.ledgerline.com is written by two tech writers in Contentful; they update pages when product managers remember to tell them. I pulled the page list this morning: the reference has 49 endpoint pages. We ship Python and Node SDKs, and we have a full sandbox environment integrators can hit. I'd like a proper audit of the reference. Honestly the pages read really well and get solid traffic, so I mostly expect polish findings.
evals.expected_output: An endpoint-level audit that censuses the 52-operation spec against the 49 published pages in both directions, diagnoses hand-maintained drift as structural in the report's opening, scores coverage as percentages with severity-tiered findings, benchmarks against Stripe/Twilio mechanisms, and promotes the full generated-docs migration.
expectations: Diffs the spec's 52 operations against the 49 published pages in both directions, checking for documented-but-removed pages as well as live-but-undocumented operations
Classifies any endpoint documented in the reference but absent from the spec or live API as a blocker (documented-but-removed destroys trust), not a minor cleanup item
Uses the spec as the census source and audits the published reference against it, never auditing the rendered pages against themselves
Recommends probing for undocumented-but-valid surface beyond the spec (gateway logs, SDK internals, or support tickets), rather than treating the spec as the whole truth
Delivers the census as a table with columns for operation, in spec, in published reference, in SDKs, and discrepancy
States in the report's first paragraph or verdict that the reference is hand-maintained, so every finding will recur until pages render from the spec
Promotes the full generated-docs migration tier because the reference is hand-maintained, instead of stopping at the lint plus contract-test default

Reports coverage as percentages against the census (operations documented, parameters fully documented, responses including at least one 4xx, error codes with cause and fix, snippet parity), not as a flat issue list
Assigns each finding a severity tier using blocker, major, and minor definitions
Benchmarks against Stripe and Twilio by checkable mechanisms (spec-generated reference, embedded personalized test keys, CI-tested snippet repository, per-endpoint error tables), not by reputation
Counts snippet parity only for samples that exercise the Python and Node SDKs, excluding relabeled curl or generic HTTP blocks

Pushes back on the expectation of only polish findings by citing that incompleteness is the measured industry norm (for example the 67.11 percent mean documentation quality or parameter examples absent from 86.95 percent of specs)
Recommends installing a standing CI gate behind the audit rather than shipping the findings as a one-off fix list

evals.prompt: We're Parcelry, a freight-booking API - 38 endpoints, OpenAPI spec exists and drives the docs site through Redocly, so pages regenerate on every merge. Docs quality still regressed twice this quarter: someone merged endpoints with no description and no error documentation at all. There is no staging or sandbox environment - every API call books real freight and costs real money, and the platform team says a sandbox is at least two quarters away. Board meeting is in 3 weeks and my VP wants 'docs can't regress again' shipped before it. Propose the fix and be specific about tooling. Also, I've read that mature API teams run contract tests, so put those in the plan for later this year.
evals.expected_output: A lint-gate-only remediation plan with a named linter and minimum ruleset, contract tests removed from the plan entirely (not scheduled for later) with an explicit re-promotion trigger, and honest framing of what a lint gate does and does not verify.
expectations: Chooses the lint-gate-only remediation tier for now
Removes contract testing from the plan entirely rather than scheduling it for later this year, because no safely-callable environment exists to run it
States the explicit re-promotion trigger for contract tests: a sandbox or staging surface a test suite may call
Justifies the removal: an option nothing can execute is not a slower option, and a parked option quietly reappears in every plan without shipping
Notes the 3-week deadline independently favors the lint-only rung as a first increment
Recommends a specific spec linter by name (Spectral, Redocly CLI, Vacuum, or RateMyOpenAPI) as an instance of the linter category
Specifies a minimum ruleset covering per-operation description and operationId, documented responses including a 4xx, and examples on parameters and schemas
Advises starting the linter at warn severity and flipping to fail-on-warn once the spec is clean
If a numeric 80 out of 100 lint bar is cited, it is labeled as RateMyOpenAPI's or Zuplo's own tool default, never as an industry average
Acknowledges the lint gate only verifies the spec describes itself, not that the spec tells the truth about the running API
Does not treat the Redocly docs site rebuilding green as a quality gate
Frames the lint gate as running in CI on every PR touching the spec, not as a one-off cleanup pass

evals.prompt: I'm putting together three slides for our CPO at Corven to fund a documentation-quality push for our logistics API. I need hard numbers: how bad API documentation is across the industry, what it costs teams, and the ROI of adding an interactive try-it console - I saw a vendor claim developers get 10x faster with one. Give me the stats with sources so I don't get shredded in the review.
evals.expected_output: A sourced set of figures where every number carries its evidence-quality label: peer-reviewed corpus measurements, survey self-reports, and vendor case studies clearly distinguished, with vendor try-it multipliers never presented as controlled results and a recommendation to measure the company's own time-to-first-call.
expectations: Cites a mean documentation quality of 67.11 percent measured across 2,529 public OpenAPI specs (OASQuali)
Cites parameter examples absent from 86.95 percent of specs
Labels the spec-corpus figures as peer-reviewed corpus measurement
Cites the Postman 2024 State of the API findings: 39 percent call inconsistent docs their biggest roadblock and/or 44 percent dig through source code to understand APIs
Labels the Postman survey figures as large-sample survey self-report, distinct from spec measurement
Presents the 1.7x to 56x faster time-to-first-call range as Postman's own vendor experiment, never as a controlled or independent result
Presents the roughly 10x faster and 225 percent registration figures as the Postman Moneris customer story, a named vendor case study
States that the try-it figures conflate the console with sandbox testing and better onboarding generally, so neither isolates the console's effect
Recommends measuring the company's own before-and-after time-to-first-call instead of reusing any vendor multiplier
Does not present the roughly 10 percent undocumented-exception crash figure as a REST or HTTP API statistic; if cited at all it is attributed as an Android platform-API study
If a time-to-first-call target appears, the under-10-minutes bound is labeled practitioner consensus, not a measured industry statistic
Every figure presented carries a named source rather than appearing as an unattributed statistic
Positions Stripe and Twilio as practitioner-consensus benchmarks compared by checkable mechanisms, not as controlled comparison evidence

evals.prompt: Hexavolt here - we sell an energy-metering API. The docs are a Docusaurus site the team edits by hand. No OpenAPI linting, no contract tests, though we do have a swagger file that's mostly right, and a staging cluster anyone on the team can safely hit. The docs pages already have language tabs for Python, TypeScript and Java - we ship official SDKs in all three - and the tabs are generated by a widget that converts our curl examples into each language's HTTP-client syntax. Leadership just approved one full quarter of docs investment and wants us to spend it shipping an embedded try-it console and code samples that feel like Stripe's. Lay out the plan.
evals.expected_output: A staged plan that refuses to jump to the try-it and samples stage first, scores the converted language tabs as zero real parity, sequences source-of-truth generation, lint gate, and contract tests before snippet parity and try-it, and notes the approved investment is the condition that promotes the full migration.
expectations: Refuses to spend the quarter going straight to the try-it console and samples while earlier stages are missing, and sequences the rollout stages strictly in order
Identifies the language tabs as converted or relabeled HTTP snippets that do not count as per-language parity because they never exercise the shipped SDKs
Scores current snippet parity at or near zero rather than crediting the three existing tabs
Puts adopting the source of truth first: the reference renders from the spec and pages stop being hand-edited
Notes the already-approved quarter of docs investment is exactly the condition that promotes the full generated-docs migration, since the marginal cost of the platform move is small
Places a spec lint gate in CI before contract testing in the sequence
Includes contract testing because a safely-callable staging environment exists, naming a property-based or spec-driven tool such as Schemathesis, Portman, or Prism
Sets the expectation that a first contract-test run on a production schema typically surfaces 5 to 15 issues, framed as normal rather than a tool failure
Achieves sample parity through x-codeSamples produced by an SDK generator (Speakeasy, Fern, Stainless, APIMatic, or OpenAPI Generator) or through a Twilio-style CI-tested snippet repository
If the Twilio snippet-repository model is described, it includes the fake API server validating every snippet in CI before merge, not just a shared snippets repo
Specifies the try-it console ships with pre-filled test credentials, the Stripe model
Warns the mostly-right swagger file must pass lint and contract verification before it becomes the source of truth, because an unverified spec passes every lie into the reference
States the parity pass condition as every shipped language having a working sample on every operation

evals.prompt: Follow-up audit for our team at Brightmast, a transit-data API. Six months ago we did what an audit recommended: the reference now renders from the spec, and Vacuum lint runs on every PR at fail-on-warn with zero errors today. We still have no environment that's safe for generated traffic - our API writes into municipal systems - so we stopped at the lint rung. Current numbers: all 41 spec operations are documented, every parameter has type, required-ness, description and example, every operation documents its responses including at least one 4xx, every error code has a cause and a fix, and there are no ghost pages for removed endpoints. Snippet parity measures 58 percent across the Ruby and Go SDKs we ship. Median time-to-first-call from our analytics is 14 minutes. Grade us against the gates - my director wants a pass/fail scorecard.
evals.expected_output: A scorecard scoped to the lint-only tier: census and lint gates pass, contract gate reported as out of scope rather than failed, snippet parity recorded as a measured percentage and finding rather than a failed gate, and time-to-first-call treated as a trend, never a gate.
expectations: Reports the census coverage gate as a pass at 100 percent
Reports the lint gate as a pass with zero errors
Reports the contract gate as out of scope at the lint-only tier, never as a failure
Explains why the contract gate is out of scope (no safely-callable environment) and states it returns to scope the moment one exists
Records the 58 percent snippet parity as a measured percentage and a finding, not a failed gate, because the team sits below the full generated-docs migration tier
Does not hold the team to the 100 percent snippet-parity gate at their current tier
Treats time-to-first-call as a trend to watch, never as a pass/fail gate on the scorecard
If the 10-minute bound is referenced against the 14-minute median, it is labeled a practitioner-consensus target and the gap flagged as a trend concern, not a gate failure
The scorecard explicitly scopes which gates apply to the remediation tier the team chose
Classifies the missing shipped-language snippets at major severity per the rubric, not blocker and not minor
Recommends a standing re-audit cadence, such as quarterly review against support tickets and docs-search analytics

evals.prompt:
Here's the reference page for POST /v1/transfers on our treasury API at Fenwick & Vale. The writer says it's our most polished page and I agree it reads beautifully - tell me if it's done.

---
POST /v1/transfers - Creates a transfer between two ledger accounts.
Parameters: source_account_id (string, required) - the funding account, e.g. acct_8f2. destination_account_id (string, required). amount_cents (integer, required) - amount in cents, minimum 1. currency (string, optional, default USD). memo (string, optional, max 140 characters).
Returns: 200 with the transfer object (a full example JSON response is shown).
Example: a complete curl request creating a $25.00 transfer.
About our ledger: Fenwick & Vale uses double-entry accounting internally; every transfer produces two ledger entries. [The page continues with four paragraphs on the ledger architecture and why we chose double-entry - it's my favorite part of the page.]
---

For context on the endpoint itself: it honors an Idempotency-Key header, and support tells me most failed calls come back as 402 insufficient_funds or 422 currency_mismatch, usually because people attempt transfers before the source account has cleared KYC verification. Give me the verdict, row by row if you have a rubric.
evals.expected_output: A row-by-row rubric verdict that the page is not done: blocker on undocumented response and error codes, majors on the missing idempotency note, ordering constraint, version statement, auth requirements and parameter depth, the architecture prose flagged as quadrant drift, and no credit given for polish.
expectations: Grades the page row by row against a per-endpoint rubric rather than giving impressionistic feedback
Flags the absence of any documented response code beyond 200, requiring at least one 4xx, at blocker severity
Requires the 402 insufficient_funds and 422 currency_mismatch errors to be documented with both cause and fix, not just their code values
Scores the error surface as its own rubric row, never folded into the examples row
Flags the missing idempotency and retry note as a finding, since the page never states the Idempotency-Key support
Flags the missing invocation-ordering constraint (source account must clear KYC verification before transfers) as a finding
Flags the four paragraphs of double-entry architecture prose as quadrant drift, explanation content on a lookup-shaped reference page, despite the user's fondness for it
Gives the architecture prose no credit toward completeness
Flags the missing version statement as a finding
Flags the missing authentication or scope requirements as a finding, since nothing states what permissions the call needs
Flags parameter-depth gaps, such as destination_account_id lacking a description or example and currency listing no allowed values
Grades the missing idempotency note and ordering constraint at major severity, distinct from the blocker-level undocumented error surface
The verdict states the page is not done, refusing the most-polished-page framing on the strength of the failed rubric rows

evals.prompt: Platform team at Quillon here - HR-tech API, 74 endpoints. Our docs regenerate from the OpenAPI spec on every merge and CI blocks the merge if the docs site build fails, so we've considered docs solved for a while. Two things came up though. First, an enterprise prospect's AI coding assistant keeps calling Quillon endpoints that don't exist. Second, someone pointed out our spec has never actually been tested against the running API - we always assumed generation keeps everything honest. I used Optic for breaking-change checks at my last job and was about to set it up here. We have a dedicated staging environment. What should we actually be verifying, and with what?
evals.expected_output: A plan that rejects the site-build check as a gate, adds a lint gate plus contract tests against staging with concrete failure criteria and realistic first-run expectations, replaces the archived Optic with a maintained differ, probes for spec-vs-live drift, and routes the coding-agent problem to its own discipline.
expectations: Rejects the docs-site-builds-green check as a quality gate, because a site rebuilds cleanly from a spec that lies about the API
States that a spec with no contract-test coverage is unverified (for example, unverified prose with better formatting) and that the generated reference inherits every lie in it
Recommends property-based contract testing against the staging environment, naming Schemathesis or a category peer
Sets the contract gate criteria as CI failing on any generated-input 500, any schema-violating response, and any undiffed breaking change
Sets the expectation that the first contract-test run typically surfaces 5 to 15 issues, framed as normal
Does not recommend Optic, noting it was archived, and recommends a maintained breaking-change differ such as oasdiff instead
Routes the AI-coding-agent hallucination problem to a dedicated coding-agent docs-optimization discipline or skill rather than folding spec-annotation rules into this audit
Recommends probing whether the live API carries undocumented-but-valid routes or parameters despite the spec existing, since spec-inference testing has found such surface in production APIs
Adds a spec lint gate for completeness alongside the contract tests for accuracy
Distinguishes the two gates' roles: the linter verifies the spec describes itself, the contract tests verify it tells the truth
Selects the lint-plus-contract-tests default rung, since docs already render from the spec and a safely-callable staging environment exists
